summary_html: Immediate state action to **protect a child in imminent danger**. Federal law (ASFA/IV-E) ties funding to court findings on **reasonable efforts**, and constitutional limits (due process, 4th/14th Amendments) constrain warrantless removals.
authority_html:
- **ASFA / SSA Title IV-E** — reasonable-efforts findings; permanency timelines  
- **CFSR (45 CFR Part 1355)** — federal oversight of removal decision quality  
- **Constitutional constraints** — enforced via §1983 actions; due process & search/seizure jurisprudence (not listed in file but governs practice)

case_law.method: v1.1.0 case-law rebuild: authorities selected per decision point, each opinion retrieved from CourtListener and read; holding and quote taken from the opinion text; independently re-verified before release. Previous keyword-matched Justia listings were removed.

key_cases.holding: The court held that an ex parte temporary detention order is not itself a final, appealable order, that henceforth the information supporting such an order must be presented by affidavit of a person with knowledge of the relevant facts, and that the mother's due process rights were satisfied because she received a meaningful opportunity to be heard at the subsequent detention hearing.
key_cases.relevance: This is the foundational Nebraska decision on what process is constitutionally owed a parent when the State takes a child into protective custody before any adjudication.
key_cases.quote: Due process principles therefore require that the mother have been given a meaningful opportunity to be heard on the issue of whether a detention order should have been issued.

key_cases.case_name: In re Interest of Borius H.
key_cases.holding: The court reaffirmed that every motion for an ex parte temporary detention order must be supported by an affidavit of a person with knowledge, held that the State must prove the requirements of Neb. Rev. Stat. § 43-254 by a preponderance of the evidence at the detention hearing, and ordered dismissal because the State adduced no evidence at that hearing.
key_cases.relevance: It states the affidavit prerequisite for taking emergency protective custody by ex parte order.
key_cases.quote: we once again state that all motions for ex parte temporary detention orders must be accompanied by an affidavit of one who has knowledge of relevant facts warranting temporary detention

key_cases.case_name: In re Interest of Carmelo G.
key_cases.holding: The court held that a delay of more than eight months between entry of an ex parte temporary custody order and the protective custody order was unreasonable and violated the mother's procedural due process rights.
key_cases.relevance: It is the leading recent Nebraska statement of the timeliness component of due process once protective custody is taken.
key_cases.quote: due process rights include the right to be free from an unreasonable delay in providing a parent a meaningful hearing after the entry of an ex parte temporary custody order

key_cases.case_name: Heartland Academy Community Church v. Waddle
key_cases.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit
key_cases.holding: The Eighth Circuit affirmed declaratory and permanent injunctive relief against a juvenile officer who removed all of a school's boarding students using stale and inaccurate ex parte petitions and, as to many children, no court order at all, rejecting his claims of judicial and Eleventh Amendment immunity.
key_cases.relevance: It is the Eighth Circuit's leading case on mass protective custody taken without individualized justification.
key_cases.quote: Waddle removed all boarding students from HCA without notice or opportunity to be heard, using stale or inaccurate information, and without exigent circumstances

key_cases.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit
key_cases.holding: The Eighth Circuit held that Rooker-Feldman did not bar the student's Fourth Amendment claim but that the social worker's good faith reliance on the ex parte protective custody order was reasonable, so he was entitled to qualified immunity on the seizure claim.
key_cases.relevance: It sets the Eighth Circuit standard for evaluating a protective seizure carried out under an ex parte order.
key_cases.quote: The ex parte order was not so lacking in indicia of probable cause as to render Diercks's reliance on it unreasonable.

key_cases.case_name: Mitchell v. Dakota County Social Services
key_cases.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit
key_cases.holding: The Eighth Circuit held that the father's and children's substantive and procedural due process claims failed because the officials' reliance on the abuse allegations did not shock the conscience and a petition, emergency hearing and post-deprivation hearing followed the removal within days.
key_cases.relevance: Protective custody must be followed promptly by a judicial hearing to survive procedural due process review.
key_cases.quote: In child removal cases, the meaningful time and manner requirement means that the state must hold a hearing promptly after removal.

key_cases.holding: The court held that a short-term ex parte temporary detention order is not final while an order entered after a detention hearing that continues to keep custody from the parent pending adjudication is appealable, and that on this record due process did not require the mother's counsel to be present at the temporary detention hearing because the juvenile court refused to take notice of that testimony at adjudication and she was represented at every later stage.
key_cases.relevance: It is the companion decided months after In re Interest of R.G. and cited alongside it in In re Interest of Borius H., fixing when an order taking or continuing protective custody becomes reviewable and what process the parent is owed at the detention hearing.
key_cases.quote: considering the procedures used in this case, due process did not require the presence of the mother's counsel at the temporary detention hearing

mandatory_reporters: Any person (universal mandatory reporting) — Neb. Rev. Stat. § 28-711(1)
Inspector General of Nebraska Child Welfare (Neb. Rev. Stat. § 50-1805)
reporting_details: Nebraska is a universal mandatory reporting state: any person who has reasonable cause to believe a child has been subjected to child abuse or neglect must report it to law enforcement or to the department on the statewide toll-free hotline (Neb. Rev. Stat. § 28-711(1)).
